title: The Cash Register Was Born From a Ship Propeller Counter
hook: The cash register came from a propeller counter a bar owner saw on a steamship

open.title: A bar owner saw a machine on a ship and changed the checkout counter
open.line: 1878, a steamship bound for Europe. An American bar owner couldn't tear himself away from a device on board.

summary: Bar owner James Ritty suspected staff of pocketing money and built the cash register after seeing a ship's propeller counter. He and his brother patented it in 1879.

text: A heavy cash register on an old shop counter.
It started with a bar owner's suspicion.
James Ritty opened a bar in Dayton, Ohio, in 1871.
He believed staff were pocketing customers' money.

panels.text: You can't catch them without proof.

text: In 1878 he took a steamship to Europe.
A device counting the propeller's turns captivated him.
Could a device like that record a shop's money too?
Back home, he began building one with his machine-savvy brother John.
The brothers got a patent on November 4, 1879.
Actually, it wasn't built for faster math.
Employees had to ring up every sale.
Pressing the total key opened the drawer and rang a bell.
The ring told customers their purchase was recorded.
Another model was the Incorruptible Cashier.
Ritty sold the business as too much work, and in 1884 it was renamed National Cash Register.
